proposed_edges.relationship: Durkheim’s sociology criticised for taking society as the cause instead of a provisional consequence, against Tarde’s “all things are society”; actor-network theory replaces “the social” with “association” (2002), a programme restated in Reassembling the Social (2005)
proposed_edges.map_label: Tarde against Durkheim: the end of the social, 2002–05
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words. "Gabriel Tarde and the End of the Social", in Patrick Joyce, ed., The Social in Question: New Bearings in History and the Social Sciences (Routledge, 2002), pp. 117–132, read in part in the author's typescript (typescript pp. 1–2, 5, 7, 10): actor-network theory is "a deliberate attempt at terminating the use of the word 'social' in social theory to replace it with the word 'association'", and "ANT actually has a forefather, namely Gabriel Tarde" (p. 1); "Instead of saying, like Durkheim, that we 'should treat social facts as a thing', Tarde says that 'all things are society'" (p. 5); "Durkheim has taken society as the cause instead of seeing that it is never more than a highly provisional consequence" (p. 10). He concedes that he had once "never enquired further than the dismissive footnotes of the Durkheimians" (p. 2). Durkheim's position is given only as Latour presents it. Reassembling the Social (2005) is unread; the author's description presents sociology as "the science of associations and not only as the science of the social". The essay appeared in a volume addressed to historians and social scientists, edited by the historian Patrick Joyce (citation only; Joyce's introduction unread). A critique of Durkheimian sociology, not of the historians who adapted it (durkheim/historical_method).

proposed_edges.relationship: An “anthropology of the Moderns”: fieldwork at the heart of modern institutions (science, economy, politics, law) that refuses to believe what the West says about itself, and distinguishes modes of existence that networks alone do not qualify (2012–13)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words. An Inquiry into Modes of Existence: An Anthropology of the Moderns (English 2013; French 2012), chapter 1, pp. 27–46, read in full: "LET US IMAGINE AN ANTHROPOLOGIST WHO HAS COME UP WITH THE IDEA OF RECONSTITUTING THE VALUE SYSTEM OF 'WESTERN societies'"; she must "focus on the very heart of modern institutions—science, the economy, politics, law, and so on—rather than on the margins" and resist "OCCIDENTALISM, a form of EXOTICISM applied to what is close at hand, which consists in believing what the West says about itself, whether in praise or criticism" (p. 27); "only a prolonged, in-depth analysis of COURSES OF ACTION" reveals the value system (pp. 27–28); "a contemporary anthropologist has to learn to talk about her subjects of study to her subjects of study" (p. 45). The author's description presents the book as the "positive version" of the question raised by We Have Never Been Modern (1991) and as "a research protocol ... very different from the actor-network theory". Reception here is limited to prize citations: the Holberg committee (2013) names anthropology among the fields his work reached, and the Kyoto citation (2021) credits Laboratory Life with opening an "anthropology of science". No review of the book was read. The reverse arrow, edge_135 (anthropology → latour), records the ethnographic method borrowed for Laboratory Life (1979); this records a later, different claim.

proposed_edges.relationship: Latour takes up Chakrabarty’s proposal that the Earth has again become “an agent of history” as a common geostory (2013–14), and answers Chakrabarty’s essay on the planet in a joint conversation on philosophies of history, where Chakrabarty finds much shared ground and offers “friendly amendments” (2020)
proposed_edges.map_label: Chakrabarty’s “agent of history” and Latour’s geostory, 2013–20
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In both authors' own words. Latour, "Agency at the Time of the Anthropocene" (New Literary History 45:1, 2014; his Holberg Symposium lecture, Bergen, 4 June 2013), read in full in the author's typescript: "the Earth has now taken back all the characteristics of a full-fledged actor. Indeed, as Dipesh Chakrabarty has proposed, it has become once again an agent of history, or rather, an agent of what I have proposed to call our common geostory" (typescript p. 3; n. 6 cites "The Climate of History: Four Theses", 2009). Latour and Chakrabarty, "Conflicts of Planetary Proportion – A Conversation" (Journal of the Philosophy of History 14:3, 2020), read in part in the authors' typescript: Latour writes in response to Chakrabarty's "The Planet: An Emergent Humanist Category" (2019), calls him "a genuine historian", and writes that "Chakrabarty's introduction of the Planetary triggered a seism in philosophy of history" (pp. 3–4); Chakrabarty answers that "Much of the ground my own thoughts move on is shared with Latour" and offers "friendly amendments" (p. 21); both credit Christophe Bonneuil for the phrase "regimes of planetarity" (n. 50). An acknowledged borrowing and a continuing exchange, not a claim that Latour's later work derives from Chakrabarty; the exchange also runs the other way, and Chakrabarty's environment edge (edge_918) records his own 2009 contribution.

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.151. Citation: "Bruno Latour has undertaken an ambitious analysis and reinterpretation of modernity, challenging the most fundamental categories such as the distinction between modern and pre-modern, nature and society, human and non-human. He has completely re-imagined Science Studies, pioneering new ethnographic methods ... His influence has been felt internationally and well beyond the social study of science, in history, art history, philosophy, anthropology, geography, theology, literature and legal studies." Les Microbes (1984) and Science in Action (1987) "represents some of the most important work in the field of science studies and in the social history of knowledge"; "In We Have Never Been Modern (1991) Latour offered his major polemical statement"; "His work in the 1980s established Actor Network Theory (ANT) as a widely used methodology"; Politics of Nature (1999) is said to propose "a parliament of things"; Inquiry into Modes of Existence (2012). The page lists the 2013 Holberg Symposium "From Economics to Ecology" (4 June 2013) in his honour and records his death on 9 October 2022. A prize committee's judgement, attributed as such.

verification.note: Profile and the opening of the citation read on 2026-10-19 for revision 1.151: Latour "revolutionized the conventional view of science by treating nature, humans, laboratory equipment, and other entities as equal actors, and describing technoscience as the hybrid network of these actors. His philosophy re-examines 'modernity' based on the dualism of nature and society. new_sources.title: Andrew Pickering, review of Bruno Latour, We Have Never Been Modern, trans. Catherine Porter (Harvard University Press, 1993), Modernism/modernity 1:3 (September 1994): 257–258.
new_sources.citation: Andrew Pickering, review of Bruno Latour, We Have Never Been Modern, trans. Catherine Porter (Harvard University Press, 1993), Modernism/modernity 1:3 (September 1994): 257–258.

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.151. "Bruno Latour's Science in Action (1987) was the most important book on science, technology and their intertwining with society published in the 1980s"; its actor-network analysis "flew in the face of technological and social determinist perspectives" (p. 257). The argument as Pickering states it: the "modern constitution" bequeathed by Boyle and Hobbes, a "program for purifying the discourses of nature and society"; "'We have never been modern,' as Latour puts it, but we found a way of thinking that we were" (p. 257). Criticism: "Latour is explaining too much with his conception of modernity"; "There is a note of complacency here at the end of Latour's book"; "I would not want to ratify what we have always done without first getting clear on the specifics of history—the history of the factory and labor, say, of gender relations, of militarism, colonialism, empire, and so on. There is no place in Latour's story for such specifics" (p. 258). He quotes the book's "Parliament of Things" (p. 144).

"I must confess that I myself never enquired further than the dismissive footnotes of the Durkheimians" (p. 2). Durkheim's position is given only as Latour presents it; Joyce's introduction is unread.

new_sources.citation: Bruno Latour, "Agency at the Time of the Anthropocene," New Literary History 45:1 (2014): 1–18.

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.151 in the author's typescript (18 pp.; typescript pages cited; author's page https://www.bruno-latour.fr/node/501.html). Prepared for the Holberg Prize Symposium 2013, "From Economics to Ecology", Bergen, 4 June 2013 (note, p. 18); the author's page, rechecked on 2026-10-19, says it was "Originally written as lecture given at the occasion of the Holberg Memorial Prize Symposium 2013" in Bergen on 4 June, with the title "Which Language Should we Talk with Gaia?", which establishes delivery. "Indeed, as Dipesh Chakrabarty has proposed, it has become once again an agent of history, or rather, an agent of what I have proposed to call our common geostory" (p. 3; n. 6 cites "The Climate of History: Four Theses"). "While the older problem of science studies was to understand the active role of scientists in the construction of facts, a new problem arises: how to understand the active role of human agency not only in the construction of facts, but also in the very existence of the phenomena those facts are trying to document?" (p. 2). "It is human history that has become frozen and natural history that is taking on a frenetic pace" (p. 13). "The prefix 'geo' in geostory does not stand for the return to nature, but for the return of object and subject back to the ground" (p. 17).

new_sources.citation: Bruno Latour and Dipesh Chakrabarty, "Conflicts of Planetary Proportion – A Conversation," Journal of the Philosophy of History 14:3 (2020): 419–454.

verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.151 in the authors' pre-publication typescript (typescript pages cited): the joint opening and Latour's pp. 1–4, and Chakrabarty's response pp. 19–22. Published online 19 November 2020 (Crossref). Joint opening: Latour responds to Chakrabarty's "The Planet: An Emergent Humanist Category" (Critical Inquiry, 2019); the piece arose from "an actual and ongoing conversation in which we have been engaged for a while" (p. 1). Latour: "Chakrabarty's introduction of the Planetary triggered a seism in philosophy of history" (p. 3); "Geohistory breaks down any claim to have a human-oriented history" (p. 4); the aim is "to give a spatial and geopolitical ground to counteract the notion of the arrow of time implied so far by traditional philosophies of history" (p. 4). Chakrabarty: "Much of the ground my own thoughts move on is shared with Latour", and he will "suggest some friendly amendments to what Latour proposes" (p. 21).
